introduction-from-writer-to-director.core: AI assistants shift engineers from typing every line to directing: specifying intent, supplying context and critically reviewing output. Judgement becomes the core skill.

first_principles.problem: Engineers either ignore AI and fall behind, or trust it blindly and ship subtle bugs.
truths: Plausible isn't the same as correct.
derivation: Describe **intent and constraints** clearly.
Give the right **context**.
**Review** like a senior engineer.
Know **where AI helps** and where it hurts.

analogy.title: A film director
analogy.story: The director doesn't operate every camera but decides what is shot and rejects bad takes.
analogy.breaks: Directors still need to know the craft deeply to recognise a bad take.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Speed from the AI, correctness from the human.

check.q: What becomes the core engineering skill with AI assistants?
check.a: Specifying intent and critically reviewing generated output.

the-tools-copilot-vs-cursor.core: Copilot-style tools excel at inline autocomplete inside your existing editor. AI-native editors like Cursor add chat over the codebase, multi-file edits and agent workflows. Pick by task.

first_principles.problem: Teams pick one tool and use it for everything, even where another interaction model fits better.
derivation: **Autocomplete**: boilerplate and line-level flow.
**Chat/agent**: refactors, explanations, multi-file changes.
Both use **context** (open files, indexes).
Match the **tool to the task size**.

analogy.title: Predictive text vs. a writing partner
analogy.story: Predictive text finishes your sentence; a writing partner can help restructure the whole chapter.
analogy.breaks: The tools converge fast; both now offer chat and agents. The interaction model matters more than the brand.

example.title: Two tasks
flow: Write a unit test body → autocomplete
Rename a concept across 20 files → agent edit + review diff

steps.label: Principle
steps.detail: Use the smallest scope that does the job.

example.outcome: the right AI interaction for each task.

check.q: Which mode suits a multi-file refactor?
check.a: A chat or agent mode with codebase context, followed by careful diff review.

prompt-engineering-for-code.core: Output quality follows input quality. Specify the language and version, the frameworks, conventions, constraints, edge cases and examples, and iterate in small steps.

first_principles.problem: 'Write a login function' produces generic, insecure code in the wrong framework.
truths: Models fill gaps with generic defaults.
Smaller steps are easier to verify.
derivation: State **role and stack** (Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2).
Add **constraints** (no new deps, must be idempotent).
Give **examples** and existing patterns.
Ask for **tests and edge cases**; iterate.

analogy.title: Briefing a contractor
analogy.story: 'Build a shed' vs. a drawing with dimensions, materials, budget and local codes.
analogy.breaks: Even perfect prompts produce errors sometimes. Prompting reduces review; it doesn't replace it.

example.title: A better prompt

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The output matches the stack and covers edge cases.

code.text:
Bad: write a retry function
Good: In Python 3.12, write a decorator `retry(n, exceptions)` with full-jitter
exponential backoff capped at 30s, using only stdlib. Include pytest tests
for success-after-retry and give-up cases. Follow our logging via `log = get_logger(__name__)`.

example.outcome: useful first drafts instead of generic ones.

check.q: Why give the model the exact library versions?
check.a: APIs differ across versions, and the model may otherwise produce code for the wrong one.

the-code-review-mindset-trust-but-verify.core: Treat AI output as a confident junior's first draft: check correctness, security, edge cases, made-up APIs and licensing. Run it, test it and read every line before merging.

first_principles.problem: AI code looks clean and compiles, yet it uses a deprecated API, skips input validation or invents a library function.
truths: The author owns the merged code.
derivation: **Read every line**; never merge code you don't understand.
**Run tests**, and add tests the AI didn't think of.
Check **security**: injection, secrets, authz.
**Verify the APIs** exist in your versions.

analogy.title: A very fast but overconfident intern
analogy.story: Great drafts in minutes, but they state wrong facts with total confidence.
analogy.breaks: Review fatigue is real. Keep AI changes small enough to review properly.

branches.label: Ownership
children: You merge it, you own it

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Code that looks right can still be exploitable.

code.text:
# AI draft
cur.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'")
# Reviewed
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = %s", (email,))

check.a: A plausible-looking function or parameter that doesn't actually exist in the library.

legal-and-copyright-risks.core: AI models trained on public code can reproduce licensed snippets, and the ownership of generated code is legally unsettled. Use enterprise tools with IP indemnity and duplicate filters, and follow company policy.

first_principles.problem: A generated snippet matches GPL code verbatim and gets embedded in a proprietary product.
truths: Law and policy are still evolving.
derivation: Enable **public-code duplicate filters**.
Prefer **enterprise plans with indemnity** and no training on your data.
Never paste **secrets or confidential code** into unapproved tools.
Follow your **organisation's AI policy**.

analogy.title: Using a ghostwriter who read every book
analogy.story: They may accidentally copy a paragraph word for word, and you're the one who publishes it.
analogy.breaks: This isn't legal advice. Consult counsel for your jurisdiction and contracts.

example.title: Rolling out an AI tool at a company
example.outcome: AI use stays within legal and policy limits.

check.q: Name one technical control that reduces licence risk.
check.a: Enabling the tool's filter that blocks suggestions matching public code.

where-ai-excels-and-where-it-fails.core: AI shines at boilerplate, tests, translations between languages, explanations and well-known patterns. It struggles with novel architecture, deep domain logic, recent APIs, subtle concurrency and security-critical code.

first_principles.problem: Using AI uniformly wastes its strengths and walks straight into its weaknesses.
truths: Models reflect common patterns in their training data.
Rare or new knowledge is weaker.
System-wide reasoning needs context models often lack.
derivation: **Use** it for scaffolding, tests, regex, docs and translations.
**Be careful** with concurrency, security and performance-critical code.
**Avoid relying** on it for novel design or post-cutoff APIs.
Use it to **learn**, but verify what it says.

analogy.title: A well-read assistant with no field experience
analogy.story: Brilliant at textbook problems, shaky on the unusual case nobody has written about.
analogy.breaks: The boundaries shift as models improve, so re-evaluate regularly.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Time saved where safe, focus where it matters.

check.q: Give one area where AI assistants commonly struggle.
check.a: For example, subtle concurrency bugs, security-critical logic or very recent library APIs.
